I built TerraSown to help farmers explore crop rotations using NASA rainfall history. I’d like to work with people interested in crop and soil research, user testing, or explaining data through maps and charts.

details:
I built TerraSown, a mobile-friendly web app that helps farmers explore crop rotations and decide what to check before planting. A farmer selects a field on a map, enters recent crops and any soil observations they have, and chooses two possible planting windows. TerraSown uses NASA POWER daily precipitation to compare rainfall over those same dates across multiple years. It displays the dates, units, data coverage, and source so farmers and advisers can see how the comparison was made.

In the public example near Ames, Iowa, TerraSown compares two 25-day windows after corn. Both windows received 38.4 mm of rain in 2025 at the app’s displayed precision. In 2024, the earlier window received 4.0 mm and the later one received 86.6 mm. Seeing both years helps a grower decide what to check about harvest timing, drainage, and equipment access before committing to a rye cover crop. Judges can replay the original NASA response and download the comparison as a CSV.

What makes TerraSown different is that it connects a historical rainfall comparison to a practical next step. Where regional research applies, the app shows the tradeoffs between keeping the usual rotation and adding a cover crop. A farmer can then save a task such as checking whether the field drains quickly enough for equipment. The goal is to help growers make better-informed decisions about keeping soil covered and adapting to changing rainfall patterns.

I designed the app around phone use, variable data availability, and the importance of local knowledge. NASA POWER provides historical climate context worldwide, while crop rotation examples stay tied to the regions where they were studied. Farmers can enter their own field observations, and missing data stays visible.

I built TerraSown with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Tailwind CSS, and Leaflet, and deployed the public demo on GitHub Pages. It runs in a standard browser without specialized hardware.I used OpenAI Codex to help identify problems in my code and troubleshoot bugs when I got stuck
